name: Policosanol

lead: Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain waxy alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane. It is sold as a cholesterol supplement and appears in metabolism-focused stacks that people use for general health.

It was developed commercially in Cuba in the 1990s, where trials reported lower cholesterol. Groups outside Cuba have not reproduced those results, though a 2018 meta-analysis reported improved lipid profiles. Cell studies suggest it may suppress cholesterol synthesis via AMP-kinase. No studies address body fat or appearance.

paras: Taken as a daily oral supplement, usually as part of a cholesterol or metabolic-health routine and sometimes included in fat-loss stacks through the general-health link.
A 2005 meta-analysis described it as well tolerated. EFSA rejected a cholesterol health claim in 2011.

angle.text: Policosanol is a sugarcane-wax supplement used for cholesterol, and people include it in metabolism and fat-loss stacks for general metabolic health. Lipid results are debated, and no studies address body fat or appearance.

lead: Policosanol is a mixture of long-chain primary alcohols, chiefly octacosanol, extracted from plant waxes such as sugarcane wax and sold as a cholesterol-lowering dietary supplement [1][2]. It was first developed commercially in Cuba [1][2]. It is not an appearance compound; the wiki lists it among fat- and metabolism-related supplements.

Early Cuban trials reported lower cholesterol [3], but a randomized trial published in JAMA in 2006 examined policosanol in people with hypercholesterolemia [4], and Wikipedia notes that groups outside Cuba have not reproduced the Cuban results [2]. A 2018 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia reported improved lipid profiles [2], and the European Food Safety Authority rejected a cholesterol health claim in 2011, according to Grokipedia [1]. No evidence was found of effects on body fat or appearance.

paras: Policosanol is a mixture of alcohols with roughly 24 to 34 carbons; in sugarcane extracts octacosanol makes up the majority, with triacontanol and hexacosanol as lesser components [1][2]. The same alcohols occur in beeswax and cereal waxes [1][2].

Laboratory studies reported that policosanol inhibits cholesterol synthesis in hepatoma cells via AMP-kinase activation [5] and modulates HMG-CoA reductase activity in cultured fibroblasts [6]. These are cell studies.

A 2002 review of placebo-controlled studies concluded policosanol lowered cholesterol in volunteers and patients with type II hypercholesterolemia [3]. A 2006 JAMA randomized trial then tested policosanol among patients with hypercholesterolemia or combined hyperlipidemia [4]; Grokipedia reports that trials in Germany and Canada failed to replicate the Cuban lipid effects [1]. A 2017 Italian position statement and a 2016 meta-analysis of nutraceutical combinations discuss its role among supplements [7][8]. A 2018 meta-analysis of 22 studies reported improved dyslipidemia, per Wikipedia [2]. No studies of policosanol for fat loss or body composition were found.

EFSA rejected health claims for maintaining normal cholesterol in 2011, according to Grokipedia [1]. Wikipedia describes it as marketed as a lipid-lowering agent in parts of the Caribbean, Latin America and Canada, and says human consumption was described as safe and well tolerated in a 2005 meta-analysis [2].
